SAF-INDUCTIVE-ON-PIN.title: {part} is wired straight to pin {pin}
SAF-INDUCTIVE-ON-PIN.why: A motor needs far more current than an Arduino pin can give (40 mA absolute maximum), and its voltage spikes can destroy the pin.
SAF-INDUCTIVE-ON-PIN.fix: Drive the motor through a motor driver such as the L298N, or a transistor with a flyback diode.

SAF-LED-NO-RESISTOR.title: {part} has no current-limiting resistor
SAF-LED-NO-RESISTOR.why: Without a resistor the LED draws far more than its 20 mA rating and burns out — and it can damage the pin driving it.
SAF-LED-NO-RESISTOR.fix: Put a 220 Ω – 1 kΩ resistor in series with the LED.

SAF-SHORT-CIRCUIT.title: {part} is short-circuited
SAF-SHORT-CIRCUIT.why: Its + and − are joined with almost no resistance: it heats up, drains at once and can melt wires.
SAF-SHORT-CIRCUIT.fix: Remove the direct connection between + and −.

SAF-OVERVOLTAGE.title: {part} gets {volts, number} V (maximum {max, number} V)
SAF-OVERVOLTAGE.why: Above its absolute maximum voltage a part is damaged immediately.
SAF-OVERVOLTAGE.fix: Use a lower supply voltage or add a regulator.

SAF-REVERSE-POLARITY.title: {part} is powered backwards
SAF-REVERSE-POLARITY.why: Reversed supply polarity destroys most electronic parts.

SAF-PIN-CURRENT.title: Pin {pin} carries {ma, number} mA (limit {limit, number} mA)
SAF-PIN-CURRENT.why: Each ATmega328P pin is rated 20 mA; 40 mA is the absolute maximum before the pin is damaged.
SAF-PIN-CURRENT.fix: Add or increase the series resistor, or switch the load with a transistor or driver.

SAF-MCU-TOTAL-CURRENT.title: The Arduino would supply {ma, number} mA in total (limit {limit, number} mA)
SAF-MCU-TOTAL-CURRENT.why: All I/O pins together share the chip's power pins, which carry only about 200 mA.
SAF-MCU-TOTAL-CURRENT.fix: Power the loads from a separate supply through transistors or drivers.

SAF-SUPPLY-OVERLOAD.title: {supply} gives at most {limit, number} mA, but its loads can draw {ma, number} mA
SAF-SUPPLY-OVERLOAD.why: When motors or servos stall, the supply voltage collapses and the board resets or the regulator overheats.
SAF-SUPPLY-OVERLOAD.fix: Give the motors or servos their own stronger supply and connect its − to GND.

SAF-FLOATING-INPUT.title: Pin {pin} is a floating input
SAF-FLOATING-INPUT.why: With nothing pulling it HIGH or LOW, the pin reads random noise.
SAF-FLOATING-INPUT.fix: Use pinMode(…, INPUT_PULLUP) or add a 10 kΩ pull-up or pull-down resistor.

SAF-NO-COMMON-GROUND.title: {part}'s − is not connected to the common ground
SAF-NO-COMMON-GROUND.why: Signals between two circuits only work when their grounds are joined.
SAF-NO-COMMON-GROUND.fix: Connect the − of {part} to Arduino GND.

SAF-BACKFEED.title: Two supplies drive the same rail: {parts}
SAF-BACKFEED.why: Supplies fighting each other back-feed regulators and the USB port.
SAF-BACKFEED.fix: Keep a single source on each rail — for example, remove the L298N regulator jumper.

SAF-OUTPUTS-FIGHTING.title: Outputs {pins} are wired together and fighting
SAF-OUTPUTS-FIGHTING.why: One pin drives HIGH while the other drives LOW: a short circuit straight through both pins.
SAF-OUTPUTS-FIGHTING.fix: Never connect two outputs; use one pin, or put a resistor between them.

SAF-COMPONENT-FAULT.title: {part} was damaged ({code})
SAF-COMPONENT-FAULT.why: It ran outside its ratings long enough to fail.
SAF-COMPONENT-FAULT.fix: Fix the wiring fault, then reset the simulation.

SAF-LOGIC-OSCILLATION.title: Logic outputs keep changing and never settle
SAF-LOGIC-OSCILLATION.why: Gates are wired in a loop that feeds an output back to an input of opposite sense, so the circuit oscillates instead of holding a value.
SAF-LOGIC-OSCILLATION.fix: Break the feedback loop, or add a clock or latch where you meant to store a value.

SAF-CODE-FLOATING-INPUT.title: Pin {pin} is read but nothing pulls it HIGH or LOW
SAF-CODE-FLOATING-INPUT.why: When the switch or sensor is not connecting it, the pin floats and digitalRead returns random values.
SAF-CODE-FLOATING-INPUT.fix: Use pinMode({pinArg}, INPUT_PULLUP), or add a 10 kΩ pull-up or pull-down resistor.

SAF-CODE-OUTPUT-CONFLICT.title: The code drives pin {pin}, but {other} drives the same wire
SAF-CODE-OUTPUT-CONFLICT.why: Two outputs on one wire fight: when one is HIGH and the other LOW, a large current flows through both and can destroy them.
SAF-CODE-OUTPUT-CONFLICT.fix: Read this pin as an input (pinMode INPUT), or wire the output to a free pin.

SAF-CODE-PWM-PIN.title: analogWrite on pin {pin}, which has no PWM
SAF-CODE-PWM-PIN.why: Only pins {pwmPins} have hardware PWM on the Uno; on other pins analogWrite just switches the pin fully on or off.
SAF-CODE-PWM-PIN.fix: Move the wire and the code to one of the PWM pins {pwmPins}.

SAF-CODE-SERVO-PWM.title: analogWrite on pin {pin} stops working while a servo is attached
SAF-CODE-SERVO-PWM.why: The Servo library uses Timer1, which also makes the PWM on pins 9 and 10.
SAF-CODE-SERVO-PWM.fix: Use another PWM pin (3, 5, 6 or 11) for analogWrite.

SAF-CAPACITOR.title: {problem, select, reversed {{part} is connected backwards} other {{part} is above its voltage rating}}
SAF-CAPACITOR.why: {problem, select, reversed {An electrolytic capacitor only tolerates about 1 V of reverse voltage ({volts} V here). Reversed, its oxide layer breaks down: it conducts, heats up and can vent or burst.} other {It sees {volts} V but is only rated for {limit} V. The dielectric breaks down, the capacitor fails and an electrolytic can vent or burst.}}
SAF-CAPACITOR.fix: {problem, select, reversed {Turn it around: the stripe (−) goes to the lower voltage, the longer leg (+) to the higher.} other {Use a capacitor rated well above the circuit voltage, about 1.5–2 times (for example 16 V or more on a 9 V battery).}}

SAF-BASE-NO-RESISTOR.title: {part}'s base is wired straight to {pin}
SAF-BASE-NO-RESISTOR.why: A transistor's base behaves like a diode to its emitter. With no resistor, {pin} pushes about {ma} mA into it, far above the pin's 20 mA, and both can burn out.
SAF-BASE-NO-RESISTOR.fix: Put a resistor between {pin} and the base: about 1 kΩ for a small transistor, 220–470 Ω for a TIP120 switching amps.

SAF-MOSFET-GATE.title: {part} only partly turns on
SAF-MOSFET-GATE.why: Its gate gets {vgs} V, but it needs about {needed} V to switch fully on. Partly on, it behaves like a resistor and heats up with the load current.
SAF-MOSFET-GATE.fix: Use a logic-level MOSFET such as the IRLZ44N, or drive the gate from a higher voltage through a gate driver or a transistor stage.

SAF-FLYBACK.title: Switching {part} off makes a {volts} V spike
SAF-FLYBACK.why: A motor or coil keeps its current flowing for a moment after it is switched off. With nowhere to go, that current drives the voltage up to {volts} V until {switch} breaks down. Each time it does, the transistor is damaged a little more.
SAF-FLYBACK.fix: Put a flyback diode (1N4007) across {part}: the striped end (cathode) to the + supply side, the other end to the transistor.

SAF-I2C-PULLUP.title: The I²C {line} line of {part} has no pull-up
SAF-I2C-PULLUP.why: I²C parts only ever pull a line low; a resistor must pull it back up. Without one, {line} sits at {volts} V and no data can get through (the Uno's own weak pull-ups are too weak for reliable signals).
SAF-I2C-PULLUP.fix: Add a 4.7 kΩ resistor from {line} to the part's VCC, or use a breakout board that has pull-ups on it.

SAF-I2C-ADDRESS.title: {parts} share I²C address {address}
SAF-I2C-ADDRESS.why: Every part on one I²C bus needs its own address. Both answer at {address}, talk over each other and the readings come back garbled.
SAF-I2C-ADDRESS.fix: Change one part's address (its address pin or jumper), wire XSHUT pins to the board so the sketch can give each sensor a new address, or move one part to another bus.

SAF-I2C-LEVEL.title: {part}'s I²C pins see {volts} V
SAF-I2C-LEVEL.why: {part} is a 3.3 V chip: its pins tolerate at most {limit} V. Pull-ups to 5 V on the same bus push current into it and can damage it over time.
SAF-I2C-LEVEL.fix: Power every pull-up on this bus from 3.3 V, or put a level shifter between the 5 V parts and {part}.
